syntheticProof.referenceHarnessCaveat: a naive reference regex also reads a <base> inside an HTML comment; the production extractor strips comments first, so a repair must extract the base AFTER stripNonContent. Recorded as a design requirement, not as a mismatch.
syntheticProof.conclusion: GENERIC_CAPABILITY_GAP_PROVEN: whenever a document carries a <base href> whose resolved value differs from the document URL, every path-relative, ../ and query-only href is resolved to a URL a browser would never request; absolute and root-relative same-origin hrefs are unaffected.

applicationRendered404.shape: the origin-root path with one query parameter (7-character key)

mechanicalReading: Because the document URL is the origin root "/", a path-relative href "x/", a root-relative href "/x/", a same-origin absolute href and even "../x/" all resolve to the SAME URL under the current code. The persisted request URLs therefore carry ZERO information about which href form the page used; they cannot confirm or exclude a base element.

The 33 single-segment 404s are byte-identical to the 404 the server returns for the site-policy file and the sitemap path: they were answered by a layer that never routed them to the application that rendered the root page. The one origin-root-path request WAS routed to the application (a 125,084-byte rendered 404). So the application is reachable at "/", and none of the 33 slug paths exists at the root of this origin.
The root document was served 200 to the same client, IP family and headers, so a blanket client block does not explain the pattern.

Either the root page publishes 34 links a browser would also fail on, or the crawler constructed paths a browser would not. Within HTML semantics, and with no redirect before the root, a <base href> is the only mechanism by which a browser resolves a relative href differently from new URL(href, documentUrl).
No successful or non-404 link-discovered page exists in this run, so nothing disproves a systematic resolution issue; equally, nothing proves one.

boundary: anchors.ts gains one PURE export, e.g. extractDocumentBaseHref(decodedHtml): string | null, run over stripNonContent(html) (so a base inside a comment, script, style, template, noscript, svg or iframe is ignored, exactly like anchors)

rootRunner.ingestFetchedPage computes the document base once per page: base = resolve(firstBaseHref, fetch.requestedUrl), falling back to fetch.requestedUrl when there is no base element or it does not parse; each anchor then resolves against that base
resolveAnchorHref keeps its signature (its first argument becomes the document base); the fragment is still cleared

admissibleUrl, the host policy, the frontier, discovery_parent_url (still the page URL), the budgets and the request order logic are untouched; a base on another registrable domain only produces off-scope URLs, which the existing scope gate refuses before any request
proposedMinimalRepairDesignNotImplemente.htmlSemantics: HTML uses the FIRST <base> element that HAS an href attribute; if that value fails to parse, the base falls back to the document URL - it does NOT fall through to a later <base>. The owner brief says "first valid <base href>"; a repair should follow the spec reading, and the owner should confirm which is intended.
preserved: the one institutional web gateway (gateway.ts) and robots.ts as its one caller
no browser, DOM or network primitive; regex over already-decoded text, as ADR 0006 requires
no page text or base value persisted
no retry and no adaptive behaviour
no new request budget: 35 page / 60 total / 8 hosts unchanged
proposedMinimalRepairDesignNotImplemente.separateObservationOutOfScope: hrefRaw is not HTML-character-reference-decoded (e.g. & in a query stays literal). It does not affect P:12 (0 of 34 URLs contain & or an entity artifact) and is not part of the minimal repair; recorded so the owner can decide separately.

fetchPolicyVersionImpact.reason: the repair changes which URLs the crawler requests from byte-identical HTML. Runs and observations carry exactly two version stamps (fetch_policy_version, rule_version); rule_version is the signal ruleset, so fetch_policy_version is the only durable provenance that can separate pre- and post-repair acquisition. A new discovery-semantics column would need a migration, which is excluded.
fetchPolicyVersionImpact.precedentNote: the 2026-08-27 anchor-hygiene fix (36d8bd5) changed anchor discovery WITHOUT a bump (v1 stayed). That was before any corpus evidence existed; the corpus now depends on per-run provenance, so that precedent should not be followed.
consequences: a v4 run can still be read but not resumed under v5, as for every earlier bump

a V5 acquisition-policy transition ledger and compatibility census would be needed; the census CANNOT be computed from persisted evidence for successful runs because no body is stored, so their v5 effect is NOT_DETERMINABLE and they stay accepted under their own recorded version
